stories.title: OpenAI might rebrand its data centers as ‘AI compute campuses’
stories.summary: Data centers are deeply unpopular. But what if we called them something else?

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: OpenAI might rebrand its data centers as ‘AI compute campuses’
sources.text: Data centers are deeply unpopular . But what if we called them something else? Axios reports that OpenAI is preparing a “PR blitz” for after the midterm elections on Tuesday, as Democrats seem likely to win back the House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, too . The company’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane told Axios that the midterms will be “a bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028,” when he expects AI to be “ the issue” in the presidential election. So OpenAI is to influence the AI debate moving forward, with Lehane discussing several proposals, including the development of AI “speed limits” ; finding ways to help people see AI as empowering them in their daily lives; pushing the U.S. to take a role in developing global standards; and yes — rebranding data centers as “AI compute campuses.” Lehane also described the conversation around data centers (a debate that has pushed Amazon and Microsoft to say they will no longer use NDAs in their negotiations with local governments ) as “good and healthy.” “Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects,” he said. sources.title: OpenAI wants to rebrand data centers as 'compute campuses' to try and win people over
sources.text: OpenAI is considering a new name for its biggest data centers as it looks to improve public perceptions of AI infrastructure amid ongoing political debate. Instead of calling them data centers, the ChatGPT maker is considering a rebrand to 'AI compute campuses' to give the facilities a name which sounds more economically positive. OpenAI hasn't directly announced these plans, however Axios reports that the changes could come as soon as this week, following US midterm elections on November 3 2026. It seems that the company is anticipating major political changes and the possibility that the Democrats regain control of the House of Representatives, which would result in a more challenging regulatory environment. OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane told Axios that he expects AI to be an ongoing political debate beyond the midterm elections. "Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects," he added. OpenAI has already been making efforts to win communities over, promising to partner with local communities to understand local needs. "We commit to paying our own way on energy, so that our operations don't increase your electricity prices," the company said at the start of 2026. Energy prices are a big sticking point for US citizens. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! A May 2026 report revealed that US states could face energy price hikes of between 6% and 29% by the end of the decades, and the US is already on course to re-open disused nuclear facilities to keep up with demand. But OpenAI's expansions are far from over. Stargate alone is a project anticipated to add 10GW of AI compute to the US by 2029, and it's still got just under halfway to go. sources.name: The Verge AI
sources.title: OpenAI is quietly renaming data centers ‘compute campuses’
sources.text: Critics say OpenAI should tackle people’s concerns about data centers, not rebrand them. Critics say OpenAI should tackle people’s concerns about data centers, not rebrand them. People hate data centers . They’re loud, resource-hungry eyesores that are so profoundly unpopular they have managed to achieve the near-impossible in today’s polarized political landscape: genuine bipartisan opposition . But what about “compute campuses”? Those sound lovely, right? OpenAI seems to be gambling that a quiet rebrand could be all it takes to defuse the growing political backlash that threatens to derail the infrastructure fueling the AI boom. OpenAI debuted the new terminology on Monday in an announcement launching its new “Grid Protectors Program.” The initiative, starting with an upcoming site in Effingham County, Georgia, aims to address concerns about the strain its sprawling AI infrastructure places on local power grids, particularly during extreme weather and emergencies. It’s a familiar data center problem. Yet in the roughly 900-word announcement, the term “data center” appeared just twice, outnumbered by “compute campus.” The initiative addresses worries about electricity use and the prospect of consumers being left to foot the bill for the AI buildout. OpenAI promises to “pay the costs we create” and “help communities keep the lights on.” Its two mentions of “data center” reinforce the connection: One references US data center capacity and electricity consumption, while the other directly compares OpenAI’s new “compute facilities” with “data centers built even a few years ago.” They’re “much different,” OpenAI says, with the new campuses allowing the company to be rather vaguely “flexible in our power demand.” The terminology appears to be new for OpenAI. A quick search of its website turned up no previous uses of the term. The timing is noteworthy, too. On Monday, Axios reported that OpenAI was planning to rebrand data centers as “AI compute campuses” as part of a policy and PR push after Tuesday’s midterms, anticipating a more hostile regulatory environment if Democrats make gains. Apparently, the rebrand couldn’t wait. Critics, however, aren’t buying it. A new name does nothing to lessen data centers’ environmental footprint , ease the burdens they place on local resources, or address the concerns of nearby residents. Activist groups who spoke to The Verge see the rebrand as a fairly transparent attempt to break free from an increasingly toxic label without meaningfully tackling what made it toxic to begin with. It fits within a broader lobbying push by Big Tech to counter souring public sentiment. “OpenAI is clearly responding to the unpopularity of data centers,” said Holly Elmore, founder and executive director of PauseAI US, a grassroots group campaigning to pause AI development. “Rebranding them ‘compute campuses’ may fool listeners once or twice but it’s not the name ‘data center’ that is unpopular — it’s the giant, polluting construction projects that apparently threatened to turn off people’s heat in the winter,” Elmore told The Verge in an email, calling OpenAI’s electricity announcement “woefully tone deaf.” “Communities that despise them will not be fooled into thinking they have transformed into something else.” Abre’ Conner, director of the NAACP’s Center for Environmental and Climate Justice, was similarly unimpressed. “This feels like an empty solution to an existing issue, which is that the data center infrastructure causes real harm,” she told The Verge . “Changing the name does not fix the problem and makes it seem like people’s health and our environment are public relations problems not environmental and climate concerns.” Conner argued that OpenAI should focus on changing its practices rather than what it calls data centers. “At a time when companies could utilize their resources to develop new models, create more transparency, and slow the infrastructure development, their solution is to just change their name.” Elmore agreed, suggesting the data center rebrand was an attempt by OpenAI to keep up with its rival Anthropic, but that it isn’t “spinning it nearly as well.” Earlier this year, Anthropic pledged to cover 100 percent of the upgrades needed to connect its data centers to power grids, including those that would normally be passed on to consumers. The company has also promised to invest billions of dollars in community projects developed with local leaders, protect local water supplies, and refrain from asking public officials to sign NDAs — a practice that has recently come under scrutiny . Anthropic said those commitments apply to both leased and owned data centers. Leased facilities currently make up most of its infrastructure, though its recent S-1 filing ahead of its IPO indicates the company wants to aggressively build its own, too, with many relying on gas . OpenAI did not respond to The Verge’ s request for comment about its decision to change nomenclature, its motivations for doing so, or whether doing so is an attempt to distance itself from the growing controversy surrounding data centers.

stories.title: OpenAI appoints Dan Driscoll as Senior Counselor for National Security Modernization
stories.summary: OpenAI appoints Dan Driscoll to advise on responsible AI for national security modernization, cyber resilience, and collaboration with U.S. allies.

sources.name: OpenAI
sources.title: OpenAI appoints Dan Driscoll as Senior Counselor for National Security Modernization

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: OpenAI hires former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll for national security role
sources.text: OpenAI has hired former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll as senior counselor for national security modernization, a newly created role at the company . Driscoll will focus on how artificial intelligence can be used to strengthen U.S. national security and cybersecurity, OpenAI said, while his updated LinkedIn profile also lists his new position. He will work with OpenAI's senior leadership and external partners, with a particular focus on helping U.S. allies adopt advanced AI responsibly. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the U.S. has "an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI," and that Driscoll's appointment would help strengthen American leadership in the technology. "National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years," Driscoll said. He added that AI could help reduce paperwork, process information and deliver answers more quickly to those working in national security. The appointment comes after Driscoll stepped down as Army secretary earlier this year after months of reported tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. An Iraq war veteran, Driscoll pushed efforts to modernize the U.S. military, including expanding access to drone and counter-drone technologies among U.S. allies, according to a previous U.S. Army announcement. Driscoll also met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in November 2025 to discuss a U.S.-proposed peace plan aimed at ending the war with Russia, according to a statement from the Presidential Office of Ukraine. At OpenAI, Driscoll will work with government officials, industry leaders, academic institutions and allied organizations to advance what the company calls "democratic AI." He will also help internal teams understand the operational needs of national security institutions, building on OpenAI's efforts to strengthen cyber resilience and protect essential services through its Daybreak program .

stories.title: Brookfield plans for a $27 billion AI data center at UK power station
stories.summary: Europe is scrambling to develop infrastructure to support the rollout of AI amid high energy and land costs.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Brookfield plans for a $27 billion AI data center at UK power station
sources.text: Brookfield is targeting a massive artificial intelligence data center in the north of England, as Europe scrambles to develop infrastructure to support the rollout of AI amid high energy and land costs. Energy company Drax Group said Tuesday it has signed an agreement with Brookfield and the asset manager's neocloud platform Radiant to jointly develop an AI data center on the Drax Power Station estate in North Yorkshire. London-listed shares of Drax were up 8.8% in early morning trading. The project is initially targeting up to 100 megawatts of capacity to be operational from the first quarter of 2028, with an additional 500 MW of capacity to be brought online between 2028 and 2031. It is then looking to secure more than 1 gigawatt of capacity at the site by an unspecified date. Brookfield estimates total investment, including semiconductors, could exceed £20 billion ($26.8 billion), with an initial £2.5 billion investment in phase 1. "This is a unique opportunity for the UK's AI ecosystem to build at scale," Radiant CEO Mahdi Yahya said in a statement. "By designing, building and operating from the UK, it will give British researchers, startups and enterprises access to frontier compute at home." The first phase of Brookfield's project in North Yorkshire will use power from the grid and target commercial customers from early 2028. The initial phase is subject to planning, regulatory and network approvals from the government and relevant agencies, alongside securing a tenant for the project, Drax said in a statement said. The company added that final investment decisions are yet to be made. While the U.S. has surged ahead on developing the huge data centers needed to power AI, Europe has been slower to break ground on the facilities. The U.K. in particular has struggled with high energy costs and challenges with long waiting times for businesses to connect to the grid. In October, it was reported that Microsoft had pulled out of a deal to anchor an Nscale data center just outside London, amid delays connecting to the country's power grid. An Nscale spokesperson told CNBC at the time that it remained "committed" to the project and was "exploring alternative power sources for the site." Unlike the U.K., the Nordics benefit from abundant power and available land. Countries in the region, like Finland, have seen major commitments to develop AI data centers this year. In September, Google said it would invest at least 13 billion euros ($15.1 billion) into AI infrastructure in the country, marking the tech giant's largest single investment in Europe.

sources.name: The Verge AI
sources.title: OpenAI pitches data center power plants as a way to protect nearby areas
sources.text: As public opinion has soured on data centers, it’s selling ‘AI campuses’ as protectors, instead of noisy polluters. As public opinion has soured on data centers, it’s selling ‘AI campuses’ as protectors, instead of noisy polluters. In an announcement on Monday , OpenAI says it will pilot its “Grid Protectors Program” at an upcoming data center in Effingham County, Georgia, where the company promises to free up to 1,000 megawatts of power during extreme weather or emergencies, enough to power air conditioners in around 700,000 homes. The announcement comes as opposition to data centers spreads across the US, in response to massive projects that have begun development and construction, frequently with little or no input from local residents. In Utah, residents protested after Box Elder County commissioners signed off on a data center expected to consume more than double the state’s peak electricity demand in 2025, and spread hot air in the desert valley surrounding the data center. Now OpenAI’s approach is to pitch the construction of power plants that feed the electricity required by the new AI data centers it’s building as “a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most.” Several states like Tennessee, Florida, Oklahoma, Oregon, and others have enacted laws that say they will prevent AI companies from passing energy costs on to residents, in addition to moratoriums and other restrictions. This is besides the environmental impacts, as a recent study by the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) said that powering proposed Texas data center projects could undo decades of air quality gains over just five years. OpenAI, which has switched to calling its AI data centers “compute campuses” in an effort to separate from their poor public reputation , claims it helps reduce costs for customers by operating year-round: “Electricity demand also rises and falls with the seasons, with different regions facing their biggest peaks at different times,” OpenAI’s announcement says. “Our compute campuses need power year-round. With the right agreements, that steady demand can help spread the grid’s fixed costs across more electricity sales, while flexibility lets us reduce demand when the system is busiest.” OpenAI says it’s going to continue working with policymakers and utility services to make “arrangements for our future campus to reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain.” Along with its data center in Georgia, OpenAI is also partnering with Oracle and SoftBank to build its “Stargate” data centers across the US, including in Shackelford County, Texas; Doña Ana County, New Mexico; and Milam County, Texas.

stories.title: Elon Musk se ríe de Sam Altman por afirmar que es terrible que tu PC de casa tenga memoria RAM: "¡La gente se merece tener su RAM!"
stories.summary: La crisis de la RAM está dando mucho que hablar. Hasta el punto de que el CEO de Tesla ha decidido cargar contra el creador de ChatGPT por sus últimas declaraciones.

sources.name: Computer Hoy
sources.title: Elon Musk se ríe de Sam Altman por afirmar que es terrible que tu PC de casa tenga memoria RAM: "¡La gente se merece tener su RAM!"
sources.text: Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google. La crisis de la RAM está dando mucho que hablar. Hasta el punto de que el CEO de Tesla ha decidido cargar contra el creador de ChatGPT por sus últimas declaraciones. Ya no es noticia decir que los precios se han disparado y comprar un ordenador nuevo o mejorar el que ya tienes cuesta cada vez más . La memoria RAM es la parte más afectada y parece que ante esto Elon Musk, CEO de X, Tesla y SpaceX, tiene algo que decir al respecto y, sobre todo, contra algo con lo que no está de acuerdo y que ha comentado Sam Altman, CEO de OpenAI. Contextualizando, durante una entrevista en el canal de YouTube Cheeky Pint , Altman defendió que no tiene demasiado sentido que cada persona tenga grandes cantidades de memoria RAM en su ordenador si apenas las utiliza . Según su punto de vista, sería más eficiente que esa memoria estuviera en centros de datos y se aprovechara desde la nube. "Desde el punto de vista de la distribución global, es bastante terrible que todo el mundo tenga una gran cantidad de la limitada memoria DRAM del mundo en su propio ordenador y la utilice un 5% del tiempo", explicó Altman. Elon Musk no ha podido quedarse callado y se ha burlado de las palabras de Altman con un meme y un mensaje en X: "¡La gente se merece tener su RAM!". Lo cierto es que las palabras de Altman tienen cierto sentido y razón. Sin embargo, que esto venga de alguien que precisamente controla una de las mayores empresas de inteligencia artificial del mundo resulta bastante insultante. Actualmente, la situación es tan crítica y los precios están tan disparados por culpa de estas compañías . A los fabricantes de chips les resulta más rentable fabricar las RAM de los centros de datos de IA que las que se usan en PC de usuarios normales debido a las fortunas que les pagan. OpenAI, por supuesto, está en ellas. Fabricantes como Samsung y SK Hynix ya han comentado en varias ocasiones que los problemas de suministro podrían continuar durante 2027 y más allá . Lenovo también ha avisado de que no espera que los precios vuelvan pronto a los niveles anteriores a 2026. De ahí que resulte bastante ofensivo que ataque precisamente a estos usuarios que buscan tener un ordenador potente, por el que, por cierto, tienen que pagar más que el resto. Muchas personas ahora mismo se encuentran en una situación muy complicada : necesitan más memoria para sus ordenadores (le den un uso o no más eficiente), pero cada vez cuesta más conseguirla. Y mientras las grandes compañías de IA compiten por hacerse con los recursos para seguir creciendo a toda costa, el usuario base que solo quiere mejorar su PC tiene que pagar más. Sin ir más lejos, hace unos días Samsung volvió a recordar que la situación está lejos de estabilizarse . Tanto esta empresa como otras afirman que el sector se está dirigiendo totalmente hacia un cuello de botella estructural que va a perjudicar todo el sector tecnológico mucho más allá del año 2026 . Los centros de datos que utilizan empresas como las grandes tecnológicas necesitan cantidades enormes de memoria para entrenar y ejecutar sus modelos. Y los fabricantes están dedicando cada vez más recursos a producir los componentes que necesitan estas máquinas. El problema es que las fábricas no pueden aumentar su producción de un día para otro. Samsung ha confirmado que ya tiene cubierta toda su capacidad de suministro de HBM4 (la memoria para la IA) para 2027 . Sus clientes ya han reservado toda la producción que Samsung espera tener disponible para ese año. También ha explicado que prevé comenzar la producción en masa de la siguiente generación, HBM4E, durante la primera mitad de 2027, con un aumento de la producción durante la segunda mitad del año. Mientras tanto, Elon Musk se posiciona en el bando mayoritario, haciendo uso de las redes sociales, para hacer creer a la gente que está a su favor. Sin embargo, hay que recordar de quién estamos hablando y que, por supuesto, también está al frente de una gran compañía de IA. Pero el odio entre Elon Musk y Sam Altman lleva años dando que hablar. Aunque juntos fundaron OpenAI hace más de una década, ahora están en polos opuestos. El break point precisamente tuvo lugar por aquel entonces. A principios de 2018, dejó la empresa y Altman asumió el papel de CEO . El lanzamiento de ChatGPT en 2022 marcó un punto de inflexión. OpenAI, bajo la dirección de Altman, se hizo con toda la atención global con su modelo de lenguaje. Mientras que Musk, quien había abandonado la compañía, vio cómo su visión sobre la IA se hacía realidad sin él. Su respuesta fue lanzar xAI, una empresa destinada a competir con OpenAI . Sin embargo, sus avances están bastante lejos de igualar el impacto de ChatGPT. Al final, esto hace que su odio, poco a poco, no pare de crecer y cualquier excusa es buena para volver a dejarlo claro.

sources.name: TechRadar
sources.title: 'The people deserve to have their RAM too!' Elon Musk mocks OpenAI Sam Altman's claim that people owning home PCs with RAM is 'terrible'
sources.text: Elon Musk has mocked OpenAI CEO Sam Altman following the latter's declaration that owning a PC with RAM is 'quite terrible' , as the components should be powering the next generation of AI data centers. In his typically irreverent manner, Musk shared a meme on X , the social network he owns, showing a version of a scene from Inglorious Basterds with a German WWII officer played by Christoph Waltz apparently hunting for people hiding sticks of DRAM. "The people deserve to have their RAM too!" Musk's meme declares. Altman made his claim during an appearance on the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, with his beliefs causing widespread condemnation and confusion across the industry. "From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time," Altman said. "You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that." Altman's comments come as consumers face rising prices for any kind of computing hardware as the demand for RAM and other components gets passed down. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! In recent months, we've seen the likes of Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan warning of continued shortages and price rises , noting, "AI hardware will stay in short supply for the next 2 to 3 years", a trend he said was "driven by persistent constraints in the underlying tech supply chain." Dell CEO Michael Dell has also voiced his belief that the memory shortage will get worse through 2027, and that these RAM woes are going to be prolonged for quite some time. Top DRAM manufacturers Samsung and SK hynix have also warned that AI-driven memory shortages will last until 2027 and beyond , with their supplies rumored to be down to fewer than 10 days of memory inventory. Interestingly, Altman reportedly recently met with about 50 senior Samsung executives in South Korea, as he looked to secure more hardware for OpenAI to expand its AI capacity. But no matter what happens, one thing that (probably) won't happen is Altman breaking into your house to steal your PC's RAM ...probably. stories.title: Build a repeatable PHP-to-Java migration engine with Kiro
stories.summary: Turn a PHP-to-Java migration from a one-time leap of faith into a measurable, repeatable process with Kiro. This post walks through a reusable engine: a mechanical discovery scanner and an eight-phase, parity-first workflow that treats the original PHP application as the specification and verifies the Java port with a parity harness.

sources.name: AWS Machine Learning
sources.title: Build a repeatable PHP-to-Java migration engine with Kiro
sources.text: When your team moves a mature PHP application to Java, you gain stronger type safety, broader library support, and more predictable scaling. A PHP codebase built over the years with Laravel, Symfony, or Doctrine carries business rules in places that are not obvious, from Eloquent traits to XML mapping files, so a structurally similar Java port can compile cleanly and still behave differently. This post shows how to turn PHP-to-Java migration from a one-time leap of faith into a measurable, repeatable process using Kiro . Kiro is an AI integrated development environment (IDE) that pairs an AI agent with your codebase to run multi-step engineering tasks with you in the loop. The approach centers on a reusable engine: a shared methodology, a mechanical discovery scanner, and an eight-phase workflow. This engine treats the original PHP application as the specification and refuses to declare the Java port correct until a parity harness verifies it. You start with an open repository, so you can run the engine yourself rather than read about it. Everything the engine knows lives in a small set of skill files, and with those files, you can run the same methodology in more than one way. Everything here is packaged as skill files: versioned Markdown capability packages that encode the migration methodology (php-to-java-migration) and the discovery scanner workflow (php-model-discovery). Because that knowledge lives in files rather than any one tool, you can run the same methodology in two ways. Kiro brings an AI agent into your editor to drive a migration step by step. Open the repository root as a Kiro workspace and the skills activate automatically when you ask Kiro to migrate a PHP application. Kiro then walks the eight-phase workflow with explicit approval gates, so you review the discovery manifest, approve the rulebook, and sign off on each phase before the next begins. It’s the mode used for every example in this post. AWS Transform is the AWS agentic AI service for large-scale migration and modernization, and it now integrates natively with Kiro. Through that integration, you can hand AWS Transform the same skill files that govern an interactive Kiro session, so discovery before translation, the parity harness as referee, and ‘ fix the loop, not the code ’ apply to an autonomous run. The engine is organized around a single principle: one shared brain, many projects. To open it, clone the repository locally, then in Kiro open a folder and select the repository root (the folder containing .kiro/). Kiro loads the skills and steering automatically, with fuller steps in “Getting started.” The workspace separates a shared methodology layer from the individual projects that use it, as shown in the following diagram. At the top is a global .kiro/ layer that every project draws on. Beneath it sit the per-project folders, each with its own PHP source, Java output, and specification sub-folder. Figure 1: The workspace is split into a shared, global methodology layer and per-project code and spec folders Those same shared skill files can be run in two different ways, shown in the following diagram. The identical eight-phase, parity-first pipeline can be driven either by Kiro (interactive, one application at a time) or by AWS Transform (agentic, at portfolio scale), and both convert PHP source into parity-verified Spring Boot Java. Figure 2: The same shared skill files drive two execution paths: Kiro (interactive, one app at a time) and AWS Transform (agentic, portfolio scale). Both run the identical eight-phase parity-first pipeline, converting PHP source into parity-verified Spring Boot Java A shared, global layer under .kiro/ holds two Skills, php-model-discovery (the scanner) and php-to-java-migration (the eight-phase playbook), plus the core-workflow.md Steering file. Each per-project folder holds its own PHP source, Java output, and spec sub-folder under .kiro/specs/, so improving the methodology once lets every project inherit the gain. The single most important rule fires before anything else: Don’t read, guess at, or hand-translate a model or entity file until the scanner has run. The scanner works in a single pass with no dependencies, as shown in the following diagram. It applies three discovery strategies to the source tokens and emits one JSON manifest, with anything ambiguous routed to a review-flag queue for a human to resolve. Figure 3: The scanner runs three discovery strategies over source tokens and emits a single JSON manifest with a review-flag queue The scanner is discover-models.php, a single-file, dependency-free PHP command-line tool that doesn’t execute the target code. It only reads source text as tokens, so it runs against apps of your choice whether its dependencies are installed. It runs three strategies on every scan: Eloquent model discovery (walking the class inheritance chain to Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Model), Doctrine attribute detection (the #[ORM\Entity] attribute), and ORM XML mapping (external *.orm.xml files). The output is a single JSON manifest. A models[] array carries every field, cast, relationship, and visibility rule, and a flags[] array appears on every entry. The scanner flags ambiguity rather than guessing. For example, a $fillable list built from a runtime expression becomes a plain-English flag, and that flag list is the human review queue. Phase 0 is preparatory: it runs the scanner and assembles the inventory. The first three phases then concentrate human expertise. Phase 1 builds the parity harness before Java is written, replaying request/response pairs against both the PHP original and the Java port. The harness must pass against working PHP and fail when you break it deliberately, because a harness that misses injected breakage is not trusted. Phase 2 seeds the rulebook and gap inventory (RULEBOOK.md, GAP_INVENTORY.md), and Phase 3 stress-tests it against representative files before committing it across the application. stories.title: Building intent-driven UI testing with Amazon Nova Act
stories.summary: Epsilon's Agentic Platform team delivers UI testing as a managed, multi-tenant service built on Amazon Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool. Tests are written in plain English and run on browsers managed by AWS, giving every product team resilient, intent-driven testing with zero per-team infrastructure overhead.

sources.name: AWS Machine Learning
sources.title: Building intent-driven UI testing with Amazon Nova Act
sources.text: To scale intent-driven UI testing across its product teams, Epsilon , a data, technology, and marketing-services company and part of Publicis Groupe , turned to Amazon Nova Act . With hundreds of millions of consumer profiles and thousands of brand relationships, Epsilon needed UI testing that could keep pace with rapid application changes. The solution could not create maintenance overhead for every product team. Within Epsilon, the Agentic Platform team (50 engineers) builds shared infrastructure so other product teams can build, deploy, govern, and run AI agents safely. With this shared platform, teams get a skills-based agent builder. They also get federated identity and pre-flight authorization, Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration, and cross-account provisioning. When a product team wants to adopt AI tooling, they get capabilities without additional configuration and without re-solving identity, security, browser infrastructure, or model integration on their own. One of those managed capabilities is UI testing . With Amazon Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), Epsilon’s platform team could deliver resilient, intent-driven testing as a service to teams on the platform. In this post, we walk through Epsilon’s architecture for delivering UI testing as a managed platform service, show the core Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool integration code, highlight a concrete 18-step test workflow, and share best practices and measured results. Epsilon’s existing UI testing practice was not broken. The team maintained a Playwright-based regression suite that validated functionality across their web applications, and it worked well. Playwright remains their regression backbone today. The opportunity Epsilon identified was additive, not corrective: The goal: layer intent-based testing on top of the existing Playwright regression suite. Deliver it as a multi-tenant platform service so that each Epsilon product team could consume through the same API surface they used for every other agent capability. Epsilon evaluated options against two requirements: natural-language test authoring (to complement selector-based Playwright tests) and managed browser infrastructure (to fit their multi-tenant platform model). With Amazon Nova Act combined with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, Epsilon could address both. Epsilon chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool specifically because it eliminates the operational burden of managing browser binaries, display servers, and session lifecycle. The Agentic Platform team had no interest in owning that infrastructure. Epsilon’s solution has three main components: a platform API for creating workflows, a background task runner for executing them, and the Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool integration that drives the browser. Epsilon’s UI testing capability follows a clear pipeline: Figure 1: Epsilon’s UI Testing Service architecture Figure 1 shows the layered architecture of Epsilon’s UI Testing Service. User requests flow from the Agent Cloud Frontend through an API Gateway with authentication and permission checks. The API layer (Django REST) exposes endpoints for workflows, executions, automation suites, and stats. The business logic layer includes a Workflow Manager, Execution Orchestrator, and Suite Coordinator. Test jobs are queued in Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) and picked up by the Runner Service running on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), which contains the Nova Act engine and a headless Chromium browser. Results, screenshots, trajectories, and HTML reports are stored in Amazon S3. The capability is exposed as a standard agent ( ui-test-agent ) with two skills: Onboarded teams consume UI testing the same way they consume any other platform agent. No additional infrastructure to manage. The onboarding process is straightforward. The platform team provisions a cross-account IAM role for the new team, registers their target application URLs, and grants access to the ui-test-agent through the existing platform API. From that point, teams create workflows, trigger executions, and retrieve results through the same interface they already use for other platform capabilities. Epsilon runs UI tests in a dedicated runner service (a FastAPI sidecar) that pins nova-act 3.x with Workflow and IAM authentication support, plus the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool client.
